accuracy.evidence: Dates and facts checked: The Taming of the Shrew c.1590-92 for an all-male company; Fletcher's The Woman's Prize, or The Tamer Tamed c.1611; Garrick's afterpiece Catharine and Petruchio, Drury Lane 1754; the 1929 Pickford/Fairbanks film, the first sound feature of a Shakespeare play, with Katherine's wink; coverture and the 1563 Homily of the State of Matrimony; quotations 'my goods, my chattels' (3.2) and 'Thy husband is thy lord, thy life, thy keeper' (5.2). AO3 wording matches AQA, Edexcel and OCR A-level specifications.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the examiner-reported context faults: bolted-on biography ('born in Stratford in 1564' sorted as bolted on), presentism (votes-for-women deck card and mastery m2), monolithic audiences ('all Elizabethans found it funny', m3), context replacing close reading (slip deck and m5), and treating a retelling such as Wide Sargasso Sea as evidence of authorial intent (m4).

lab_distinct.evidence: One dealt card at a time is dragged into bins across five different decks: production vs reception, a four-slot reception timeline, sharpens vs bolted on, three critical lenses, and sound vs slip. This differs from flagbard (Macbeth production context only), flaginfer and every sorter lab, and passes the 30% shingle distinctness gate.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each deck builds one skill in order: name the two contexts, see that the same words met four audiences across 400 years, judge whether a context sentence changes the reading of a line, see one line read through three lenses, then catch slips. Feedback after every drop explains why the card belongs where it does, tied to a quotation or date.

predictions.evidence: Predictions come before the action on step 0 (is meaning fixed by the writer's time?), step 1 (was the taming accepted at first? answer: answered within about 20 years by Fletcher) and step 4 (is judging the play by modern values a sound move?), so learners commit and then test their view against the decks.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The challenge mixes new texts (Merchant of Venice after 1945, Wide Sargasso Sea, Othello reception, coverture) with 13 specific feedback messages that name the error, e.g. explaining that post-1945 stagings are reception, not production, and that Rhys's novel is a reinterpretation, not proof of Brontë's intent.

readability.evidence: Learner audience: kid explanation Flesch-Kincaid grade 3.2 (limit 6.5) and adult 6.5 (limit 9.5), with short sentences, terms defined at first use (context of production, context of reception, coverture, presentism) and on-canvas card text kept under about 25 words.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a concrete example or assessment fact: the Shrew reception history, coverture with the chattels quotation, AO3 wording, Jauss's horizon of expectations, and a named list of four common mistakes. No generic praise or padded summaries; practice and mastery explanations each give a reason.

mobile.evidence: Walkthrough on iPhone 13 and desktop: 6 steps, 5 tasks and the challenge completed on both with no console errors. Cards and bins are large drag or tap targets, every bin has a matching button below the canvas, and screenshots show card text wrapping cleanly inside the card at phone width.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core reports zero violations in light and dark themes on both devices. The canvas has an aria-label and a live text description of the current card, every drag has a button alternative, dark text sits on the amber card for strong contrast, and reduced motion removes the card fly-in.
